questions.title: SECTION A: COMPREHENSION — Questions on Text A (Article: 'The Price of the Perfect Post')

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to paragraph 1. Identify the setting and the central concern introduced by the writer. Use your own words.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (Setting): South Africa — from townships to suburbs; morning routine (before speaking to family).
Mark 2 (Central concern): Smartphones have colonised the first and last moments of young people's days / youth are dominated by screen notifications before real-world interaction.
[Award 1 mark each. Accept paraphrases.]

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to paragraph 2. Comment on the effect of the word 'sobering'. What does this word choice reveal about the writer's attitude?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (Meaning): 'Sobering' means making one serious or clear-headed / alarming or chastening.
Mark 2 (Attitude): Word choice reveals the writer has a concerned / serious / alarmed attitude — the data should shake the reader out of complacency.
[Must identify meaning AND attitude for both marks.]

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to paragraph 3. In your own words, explain how social media platforms exploit human psychology. Why are teenagers particularly at risk?
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1–2 (Exploitation): Social media platforms trigger dopamine releases (through likes, comments, shares) — the same neurochemical activated by gambling or sugar. This exploits the human need for social validation. (Must mention dopamine for full 2.)
Mark 3 (Teen vulnerability): Teenagers are at particular risk because their prefrontal cortices (governing impulse control and long-term thinking) are still developing — they are more susceptible to addictive feedback loops.
[Award up to 2 for exploitation explanation; 1 for teen vulnerability.]

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to paragraph 4. Explain what Dr Khumalo means by 'comparing their unfiltered selves to everyone else's highlight reel'. Use your own words.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1–2: Dr Khumalo means young people measure their real, imperfect lives against the carefully selected, edited best moments others post online.
Mark 3: This creates an unfair comparison: the scroller sees an idealised artificial version of others' lives measured against their own messy reality.
[Award up to 2 for the explanation of the metaphor; 1 for development of the unfairness/contrast.]

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to paragraph 5. What is 'social comparison injury'? Discuss how the writer suggests this condition is made worse by South Africa's specific social context.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1–2 (Definition): 'Social comparison injury' is a persistent sense of inadequacy caused by measuring oneself against others online.
Mark 3 (SA context): Made worse in South Africa because existing challenges — economic inequality, racial tension, high unemployment — mean many young people lack the support structures to process additional psychological pressure.
[Award 2 for definition; 1 for SA context.]

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to paragraphs 6 and 7. The writer acknowledges benefits of social media before returning to criticism. Is this approach effective? Critically discuss, supporting your answer with evidence.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1–2 (Position with reasoning): YES, effective — Acknowledging benefits (community for marginalised youth) prevents the writer appearing one-sided and strengthens credibility / ethos.
Mark 3 (Persuasive effect): The concession makes the final criticism ('something must give') more persuasive because readers cannot dismiss it as uninformed.
Mark 4 (Evidence): Quotes/references such as 'But critics respond that the same platforms which offer community also commodify vulnerability' — a swift return to critique.
[Open-ended evaluation. Award marks for any reasoned position with evidence. Candidate may also argue NO if reasoning and evidence are sound.]

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss the tone of the article as a whole. Identify at least TWO tone words and justify your choices with evidence from the text.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark per valid tone word + 1 for evidence (must have BOTH for each mark; max 2 tone words; total 3 marks).
Valid tone words and supporting evidence:
• Concerned/alarmed: 'sobering'; 'unsustainable'.
• Critical: Platforms 'architecturally designed to exploit'; critique of policymakers.
• Urgent: 'Something must give'; 'the current situation is unsustainable.'
• Measured/analytical: Benefits acknowledged — not hysterical.
[Overall tone is concerned / critical / urgent. Accept any valid combination with textual evidence.]

subQuestions.questionText: Is the writer objective in this article? Motivate your answer by referring to the text.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (Position): NOT fully objective — clear position that social media is harmful and change is needed.
Mark 2 (Evidence): 'Something must give — either platforms must be held accountable'; statistics selected to support concern; defenders given less space.
Mark 3 (Nuance): PARTIALLY objective — paragraph 6 acknowledges benefits; some attempt at balance. But conclusion reveals normative stance.
[Award 1 for clear position; 1 for explanation; 1 for textual evidence. Accept a 'partially objective' answer if well-supported.]

questions.title: SECTION A: COMPREHENSION — Questions on Text B (Cartoon: 'The Filtered Life')

subQuestions.questionText: Describe what is happening in Panel 1 (left) of the cartoon. Identify at least TWO visual details. (Refer to the cartoon 'The Filtered Life' in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Award any TWO (1 mark each):
• A teenager holding a phone and taking a selfie.
• Bright colourful background with sunshine and flowers — idealised online world.
• Floating hearts and stars — social media 'likes'.
• Speech bubble: '#PERFECT'.
• Teen appears happy/smiling in Panel 1.
[Must reference VISUAL DETAIL, not just 'teen on a phone'.]

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the humour in the cartoon. How does the contrast between the two panels create a comic or ironic effect?
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1–2: Humour/irony arises from the extreme contrast: Panel 1 shows a colourful, idealised scene (#PERFECT) while Panel 2 shows the identical teen in a grey, dull, messy room with '0 Likes'. The gap between polished online image and mundane offline reality is so extreme it becomes comic — the '#PERFECT' caption is ironic given Panel 2.
[Award 2 marks for clear identification of contrast AND explanation of comic/ironic effect.]

subQuestions.questionText: What is the message of the cartoon? How do the visual elements support this message?
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1–2 (Message): Social media creates a false, curated version of reality. Young people perform happiness online while real lives may be ordinary, lonely, or difficult.
Mark 3 (Visual support): The two contrasting panels — bright/idealised vs grey/mundane — visually enforce the gap. The '#PERFECT' caption in Panel 1 is ironic given Panel 2 — this verbal/visual tension carries the message.
[Award 2 for message; 1 for visual support analysis.]

questions.title: SECTION A: COMPREHENSION — Questions on Both Texts

subQuestions.questionText: Both Text A and Text B address the impact of social media on young people. Identify ONE way in which they agree and ONE way their approaches differ. Quote evidence from both texts.
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1–2 (Agreement): Both texts agree social media creates a false version of reality. Text A states young people compare 'their unfiltered selves to everyone else's highlight reel'; the cartoon shows a '#PERFECT' online life contrasted with dull reality.
Marks 3–4 (Difference): Text A takes a formal, analytical approach using statistics and expert opinion; the cartoon uses humour and visual contrast to deliver the same message more immediately.
[Must quote from BOTH texts for full marks. Difference must relate to approach/form, not content.]

subQuestions.questionText: Read the passage 'Understanding the Teenage Brain' carefully. The passage identifies what teenagers need from the adults around them and the unique strengths teenagers possess. Summarise these points in a single fluent paragraph of 7–8 points. Your summary must not exceed 90 words. Write in full sentences and use your own words as far as possible. NOTE: Marks will be awarded as follows: Content: 7 marks (one mark per valid point); Language: 3 marks (accuracy, fluency, own words).
subQuestions.memoText:
CONTENT POINTS — Award 1 mark each (max 7):
1. Teenagers need meaningful connection / genuine relationships.
2. They need genuine challenge — to be stretched and trusted with real responsibility.
3. They need the belief that they are trusted by adults around them.
4. They benefit from spaces for honest conversation.
5. They need the freedom to fail and recover — learning through mistakes.
6. Teenagers possess remarkable creative energy.
7. They have strong moral sensitivity and a sense of justice.
8. They demonstrate willingness to act on principle at personal cost.
9. History shows teenagers have changed the world (e.g. 1976 Soweto; 2019 climate strikes).

LANGUAGE AWARD — 3 marks:
• 3 marks: Fluent paragraph. Own words throughout. No copying. Within 90 words. Ideas flow logically.
• 2 marks: Mostly own words. Minor copying OR slightly over limit. Generally fluent.
• 1 mark: Significant copying OR poor construction OR well over limit.
• 0 marks: No own words. Passage copied. No paragraph structure.

[Total: 7 content + 3 language = 10 marks.]

questions.title: SECTION C: LANGUAGE STRUCTURES AND CONVENTIONS — Question 3: Advertisement (MindfulSA)

subQuestions.questionText: What does the headline 'YOUR SCREEN IS NOT YOUR LIFE' mean in the context of this advertisement? Explain fully. (Refer to the MindfulSA advertisement in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Marks 1–2: The headline means that although teenagers spend significant time on phones, a screen cannot replace real life, real relationships, or genuine experiences.
[Must address MEANING. Award 1 for paraphrase + 1 for development.]

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to the image in the advertisement. Discuss how the visual choice of showing a phone with a cross through it effectively communicates the message.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: The phone with a cross (X) through it is a universal symbol of prohibition / 'do not use this'. Communicates immediately without words that excessive phone use is discouraged.
Mark 2: Effective because it works across language barriers; the red X conveys urgency and warning, emotionally reinforcing the headline.

subQuestions.questionText: Identify and explain ONE persuasive technique used in the body text. Quote from the advertisement to support your answer.
subQuestions.memoText:
Accept any ONE of the following techniques:
• Statistics as emotional appeal (e.g. '6hrs average daily screen time'; '73% report feeling anxious without phone'; '2x more likely to feel lonely').
• Appeal to fear (links excessive screen time to 'anxiety, depression, and reduced academic performance').
• Direct address ('you') — engages reader personally ('Every notification pulls you further from the people who matter most').
• Tricolon slogan ('Put it down. Look up. Live.').
Mark 1: Technique named (or clearly described).
Mark 2: Explained with a quotation from the advertisement.

subQuestions.questionText: Comment on the effect of the font/text style used in the advertisement. How does typography contribute to its impact?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Large, bold, uppercase headline creates visual emphasis and commands attention immediately.
Mark 2: Bold creates authority and urgency; contrast between the large headline and smaller body text creates hierarchy, guiding the reader's eye.

subQuestions.questionText: Who is the target audience of this advertisement? Motivate your answer with reference to at least TWO features.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (Audience): South African teenagers / youth / parents of teenagers.
Mark 2 (Evidence — any TWO): statistics reference 'South African teenagers'; slogan uses short imperatives aimed at youth; references anxiety/depression/academic performance; the digital detox challenge is youth-oriented.
[Must name audience AND give two evidence points.]

subQuestions.questionText: Consider the slogan 'Put it down. Look up. Live.' Explain why this slogan is effective.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for any TWO of the following:
• Short punchy imperatives — memorable and energetic.
• Three-part parallel structure (tricolon) creates rhythm.
• 'Live' as the final word equates putting down the phone with truly living.
• Direct and personal without being preachy.

questions.title: SECTION C: LANGUAGE STRUCTURES AND CONVENTIONS — Question 4: Visual Text / Poster (World Mental Health Day)

subQuestions.questionText: What is the purpose of this poster? Identify at least TWO features that reveal this purpose. (Refer to the World Mental Health Day poster in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (Purpose): To raise awareness about the mental health risks of excessive screen use; to persuade young people to limit their screen time.
Mark 2 (Features — any TWO): warning statistics box / helpline number / 'What You Can Do' action steps / World Mental Health Day label.
[Must identify purpose AND two supporting features.]

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to the dominant image (the brain and the phone). Explain what this image communicates and how it supports the message.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: The brain-and-phone image communicates that technology is interfering with / controlling the mind / mental health.
Mark 2: Effective because the brain represents identity/wellbeing; the phone with chain represents digital addiction; the lightning bolt breaking the chain represents liberation — directly supporting the message of taking control of one's mental space.

subQuestions.questionText: Comment on the use of colour in the poster. How does the colour scheme contribute to the overall impact?
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Dark navy/blue background creates a serious, ominous mood — reinforcing the gravity of the issue.
Mark 2: Gold text stands out, making key messages immediately visible; the yellow helpline box creates urgent contrast. Overall the colour scheme is authoritative without being alarmist.
[Award marks for specific colour analysis tied to effect.]

subQuestions.questionText: Identify ONE fact and ONE opinion in the poster. Quote evidence for each.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (FACT): '67% of South African teens check their phone within 5 minutes of waking up every morning.' (verifiable statistic). Also accept: 'Only 1 in 3 South African teens sleeps 8+ hours per night' or 'Teens who use social media 3+ hours daily are twice as likely to report poor mental health.'
Mark 2 (OPINION): 'Seeking help is a sign of strength' (normative/value claim) OR any other clearly evaluative statement (e.g. 'Take control of your mental space').
[Award 1 for correctly identified + quoted fact, 1 for correctly identified + quoted opinion.]

questions.title: SECTION C: LANGUAGE STRUCTURES AND CONVENTIONS — Question 5: Language Structures and Editing

subQuestions.questionText: The word 'social' is an adjective. Identify the parts of speech of: (a) changed (b) simply (c) pressing.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (a): 'changed' — verb (past participle/past tense).
Mark 2 (b): 'simply' — adverb.
Mark 3 (c): 'pressing' — adjective.
[Award 1 mark each.]

subQuestions.questionText: Choose the correct option for error [A]: 'Social media have' OR 'Social media has'. Motivate your choice.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (Choice): 'Social media HAS changed…' — 'social media' is treated as a singular collective noun.
Mark 2 (Motivation): Provided motivation explains the singular collective treatment.
[Also accept 'HAVE' with the motivation that 'media' is plural of 'medium' — both are defensible. Answer alone = 1 mark; answer + motivation = 2 marks.]

subQuestions.questionText: Error [B] is a word-choice error. Identify the error and write the correct word.
subQuestions.memoText: Mark 1: Error: 'they're' → correct word: 'their' (possessive pronoun).

subQuestions.questionText: Rewrite the sentence containing error [C] beginning: 'Although young people are not simply lazy or irresponsible…' Make only necessary changes.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct rewrite: 'Although young people are not simply lazy or irresponsible, the platforms are designed to be addictive.'
[Must begin as specified; meaning preserved; grammatically sound.]
[Award 1 mark if beginning is correct but the sentence is awkward; 2 marks for a complete, correct rewrite.]

subQuestions.questionText: Identify the error at [E] and rewrite the relevant portion correctly.
subQuestions.memoText: Mark 1: Error: 'there' → correct: 'their'. Corrected portion: '…failed to include digital literacy in their curriculums.'

subQuestions.questionText: Rewrite [G] in indirect (reported) speech, beginning: 'Dr Khumalo told her colleague that…'
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct rewrite: 'Dr Khumalo told her colleague that they needed to teach young people how to use those tools wisely.'
Key changes: 'we' → 'they'; 'need' → 'needed'; 'these' → 'those'; inverted commas removed.
[Award 1 mark for correct pronouns/tense; 1 mark for removing inverted commas and changing 'these' to 'those'.]

subQuestions.questionText: Give a synonym for 'pressing' as used in the final sentence.
subQuestions.memoText: Mark 1: Any ONE of: urgent / critical / crucial / serious / vital / important.

subQuestions.questionText: Give the antonym of 'wisely' as used in the passage.
subQuestions.memoText: Mark 1: Any ONE of: foolishly / unwisely / recklessly / irresponsibly.

subQuestions.questionText: Add an appropriate prefix to 'responsible' to change its meaning to the opposite.
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Prefix 'ir-' → 'irresponsible'.
[Only 'irresponsible' is correct.]

subQuestions.questionText: Identify and correct the redundancy in: 'She repeated the question again because no one had answered.'
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1: Redundancy is 'repeated' and 'again' (to repeat already means to do again).
Corrected (either accepted): 'She repeated the question because no one had answered.' OR 'She asked the question again because no one had answered.'
[Award 1 mark if redundancy is identified AND a correction is provided.]

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the meaning of the idiom: 'to burn the midnight oil'.
subQuestions.memoText: Mark 1: To work or study very late into the night / to stay up late working hard.

subQuestions.questionText: The following sentence contains an ambiguity. Rewrite it to remove the ambiguity, choosing ONE meaning: 'Lerato watched the teacher correct the papers in her room.'
subQuestions.memoText:
Mark 1 (Identify ambiguity): It is unclear whether Lerato or the teacher was in 'her room'.
Mark 2 (Unambiguous rewrite — accept ONE):
• If Lerato's room: 'From her room, Lerato watched the teacher correct the papers.'
• If teacher's room: 'Lerato watched the teacher correct the papers in the teacher's room.'
[Award 1 for identifying the ambiguity; 1 for a clear unambiguous rewrite.]
